title: The AI Writes the Code, the Student Writes the Model: A Theory and Measurement Programme for Learning by Construction with Generative AI
content: Generative artificial intelligence can turn a sentence of ordinary language into working code, and upper-secondary students have begun to use it for exactly that. Schools have answered mostly with rules about permission, and the AI-literacy literature has asked what students should understand about these systems. Neither line of work tells a teacher how to design a lesson in which students build software with AI and come away understanding the subject the software is about. This article develops a theoretical framework for that design problem and equips it for empirical test. The framework, Code-to-Learn with Generative AI (CtL-GenAI), is built for learners aged roughly fifteen to eighteen and rests on a synthesis of constructionism, cognitive load theory, self-regulated learning, the ICAP model, productive failure, and sociocultural accounts of scaffolding. Its organising claim is that the AI may write the code while the student must write the model. The article makes that claim testable in three ways. First, it defines model authorship as a construct with four facets and four ordered levels, each with observable indicators, and specifies a partial-credit measurement model whose unidimensionality and cumulativity are themselves falsifiable. Second, it formalises the outcome the field has been failing to measure: supported performance, unsupported performance and delayed transfer are distinguished, the assistance-removal gap is defined as their difference, and the central prediction is stated as a moderation of that gap by task design rather than as a main effect. Third, it recasts verification of AI output as a signal-detection problem, separating discriminability from response criterion, which explains why verification teaches only learners who already command enough of the domain to detect error. An evidence audit of twenty-four studies published between 2021 and 2026 locates what has and has not been tested, and six hypotheses are stated with designs, measures, competing explanations and falsification criteria. Full research instruments are supplied. Whether generative AI helps or harms learning turns on how the task is designed rather than on whether the tool is present, so the unit of analysis for research and policy should be the task.
